strengths: Addresses a genuinely novel and challenging application domain—dynamic 3D fire reconstruction—that is largely under-explored in computer vision and is difficult due to fire's emissive, semi-transparent, and high-frequency nature.

The pipeline design is thoughtful: separating the static background (vanilla 3DGS with stereo-monocular depth fusion) from the dynamic fire, and using a FreeTimeGS-style representation with per-Gaussian lifetime and linear velocity, is a sensible way to handle the under-constrained 3-view setting.

The flow-based initialization of dynamic Gaussians from fused multi-view dense optical flow (Eqs. 5-8, Tikhonov-regularized) is a reasonable technical contribution that the ablation (RandFlow) shows matters for quality.

The low-cost LED/ESP32 hardware synchronization pattern exploiting rolling-shutter artifacts for sub-frame temporal alignment is a clever and practical solution for commodity cameras, and the rolling-shutter delay modeling (Eq. 9) is a nice touch.

A new real-world fire dataset (17 sequences, diverse fuels such as propane, wood, gasoline, cardboard, paper; 400 Hz capture) with per-scene results and promised public release is a useful community contribution.
Ablations over rolling shutter, synchronization, flow initialization, and static/dynamic separation provide evidence about which components matter.
The paper is clearly written and well-organized, with informative qualitative visualizations (Figs. 1, 6, 9) and per-scene supplementary tables.
Reproducibility is addressed via promised code, dataset, and detailed implementation/hardware sections.
weaknesses: The method is largely a composition of existing techniques (3DGS, FreeTimeGS, MEMFOF optical flow, DepthAnythingV2, COLMAP, PatchMatchStereo); the fundamental algorithmic novelty beyond pipeline integration and the flow-based initialization is limited, which weakens the case for a top-tier venue on originality grounds.

The depth evaluation (RMSE_depth) is conceptually circular: the 'ground-truth' depth is itself a monocular depth estimate (DepthAnythingV2) that is acknowledged to be unreliable for transparent/emissive flames. Since flame geometry is not well-defined, using this as the primary geometric metric is questionable and may overstate the method's geometric fidelity.

Only two baselines are evaluated (both 4DGS variants: Wu et al. and Yang et al.), both run with their author-default parameters on the authors' own dataset. A broader set of dynamic-Gaussian and dynamic-NeRF baselines would strengthen the comparison, and the near-universally large gap in favor of the proposed method invites scrutiny of the experimental setup.

The paper's own ablation undermines two of its headline contributions: the rolling-shutter modeling (GlobalShutter) shows 'no clear impact regarding the quantitative evaluation,' and the synchronization ablation (NoSync) shows only modest degradation. This suggests the claimed hardware and rolling-shutter contributions may not be as central to performance as presented.

Fire is emissive and semi-transparent, violating the radiance-field / opaque-Gaussian assumption. The manuscript acknowledges this but provides only limited treatment of the physical modeling (e.g., emission, view-dependent transparency), so it is unclear how physically faithful the reconstructed 'geometry' and radiance actually are versus merely photo-plausible.

Novel-view-synthesis generalization is demonstrated only on the authors' self-captured dataset with a held-out view split; there is no evaluation on a public benchmark or independent data, limiting claims of generalization.

The conceptual framing of '3D reconstruction of flames' is ambiguous: it is unclear what an appropriate ground-truth geometry for a flame would be, and the reported per-Gaussian velocities are not validated against any independent motion measurement.

Some methodological details are under-specified (e.g., how the dynamic/static boolean assignment and the static/dynamic boundary is enforced, and how the minimum-intensity-projection background estimation behaves when flames are not brighter than the background or when the background itself varies).

strengths: Addresses a challenging and novel problem: reconstructing high-frequency dynamic flames in 3D from only three commodity cameras, with applications in graphics, safety, and fire analysis.

Proposes a complete pipeline that combines static/dynamic separation, dense optical-flow-based 3D initialization, FreeTimeGS-based dynamic Gaussians with lifetime and linear velocity, rolling-shutter-aware rendering, and a custom hardware synchronization pattern.
Introduces a real-world fire dataset (17 sequences, three synchronized 400 Hz GoPro views, varied fuels) and promises code/data release, which is a valuable contribution to the community.

Provides quantitative and qualitative comparisons against two 4DGS baselines, showing improved flame-masked PSNR/SSIM and substantially lower depth RMSE; ablations validate the importance of synchronization, flow-based initialization, and separate static optimization.
The paper is clearly written, well illustrated, and includes a candid discussion of limitations (flow errors, linear velocity model, static/dynamic assumption, synchronization residuals).
weaknesses: The core 3D flow fusion is technically questionable: the constraint (F(x)-u_i(x))^T u_i(x)=0 does not enforce that the 3D flow projects to the observed 2D optical flow; it only constrains the component along u_i. A correct projection constraint should use the image Jacobian (e.g., J_i F = f_i). This weakens the justification for the flow-based initialization, which is a main contribution.

The rolling-shutter modeling is not empirically supported by the ablation: the GlobalShutter variant performs comparably or slightly better than the full method in Table 2 (e.g., PSNR_flame 27.48 vs 27.46, RMSE_depth 0.0408 vs 0.0412), and the text acknowledges no clear quantitative impact. Thus one of the four claimed contributions is not convincingly validated.

Evaluation is limited: only two 4DGS baselines are compared on the authors' own dataset, with no comparison to FreeTimeGS (the base representation) or other dynamic Gaussian/NeRF methods, and no standard benchmark. The method has lower full-frame PSNR/SSIM than 4DGS (Yang et al.), and the trade-off between background fidelity and flame reconstruction is not fully analyzed.

Depth evaluation relies on monocular depth predictions after linear alignment as pseudo-ground-truth rather than true 3D measurements, so the claimed geometric plausibility of the depth is only weakly validated.

The static/dynamic separation assumes flames are brighter than the background and that the background is static; this may fail for sustained fires, smoke-heavy scenes, or fire-induced illumination changes. The dataset, while welcome, covers only 17 mostly controlled-burn scenes and three cameras, so generalization to larger or wildland fires is unclear.

Optical flow on transparent, emissive flames is inherently noisy, but there is little analysis of flow quality or sensitivity beyond the RandFlow ablation; errors in the flow field may propagate into the 3D motion field.

strengths: Addresses an underexplored and practically relevant problem: sparse-view (3-camera) spatiotemporal reconstruction of a volumetric, semi-transparent, high-frequency phenomenon (fire) using commodity hardware, with plausible application value for fire-safety and wildfire scenarios.

The pipeline is technically coherent and well-engineered end-to-end: static/dynamic decomposition, stereo (PatchMatchStereo) + monocular (DepthAnythingV2) depth fusion with linear alignment and a depth-regularization term, per-view optical flow (MEMFOF) fused into a 3D voxel flow field, and flow-initialized FreeTimeGS primitives with lifetime/velocity parameters.

The real-world dataset is a genuine asset: 17 scenes, 4 fuel types, varied backgrounds, 3 synchronized 400 Hz GoPro captures, per-scene annotations, and an LED/Gray-code synchronization scheme. Releasing this (and code) is a concrete community contribution.

The paper is generally readable, the pipeline figure (Fig. 2) and intermediate-data figure (Fig. 4) clarify the stages, and the per-scene tables (Tabs. 4–10) plus the reported depth/PSNR/SSIM masked metrics give a reasonably transparent view of performance.

The qualitative comparisons (Fig. 9) and the discussion of why 4DGS baselines overfit the background are useful, and the rolling-shutter derivation (Eq. 9) and sub-frame timing discussion show attention to a real practical issue.
The writing flags limitations explicitly (optical-flow errors, linear-velocity model limitations, static/dynamic separation assumption) and proposes sensible future directions.
weaknesses: Contribution type mismatch: the paper is framed as an algorithmic contribution, but the technical core is an assembly of existing components (FreeTimeGS, MEMFOF, DepthAnythingV2, COLMAP, vanilla 3DGS) applied to a new domain. Assessed as Applied/Systems work, the evidence bar is not met either, because the evaluation does not isolate what the new components actually buy (see below).

Novel-view synthesis is claimed repeatedly, but the quantitative protocol does not evaluate novel views: Sec. 5 only removes every 8th frame (a temporal split) from the same three camera poses. No held-out camera viewpoint is used for any metric, so the central 'novel view synthesis' claim is unsupported quantitatively. The supplementary video (camera poses 'leaving' the training set) is qualitative only and is not quantified.

Two of the four advertised contributions are not supported by the authors' own ablations. Table 2 shows GlobalShutter (rolling-shutter rendering disabled) at PSNR_flame 27.48 / SSIM 0.8472 vs. 27.46 / 0.8469 for the full method — i.e., no measurable effect — and the text concedes 'no clear impact regarding the quantitative evaluation.' Similarly, NoSync differs from the full model by only ~0.3 dB, and the claimed microsecond synchronization precision is never independently validated. Contributions (3) and (4) in the introduction are therefore asserted rather than demonstrated.

The depth metric is essentially self-referential. RMSE_depth is computed against a monocular DepthAnythingV2 prediction after linear alignment (Eqs. 1–2), while the same aligned monocular depth is used as a regularization term during optimization (Eq. 3). Reporting the proposed method as dramatically better (0.0412 vs. 0.2655/0.2749) on a quantity it was explicitly trained to match is not a meaningful geometric accuracy measure; no LiDAR, structured-light, or simulation ground-truth depth is used.

The full-frame metrics actually favor the 4DGS (Yang et al.) baseline (PSNR 35.29 vs. 33.61; SSIM 0.9623 vs. 0.9504; LPIPS 0.0392 vs. 0.0492). The paper dismisses this as baseline overfitting, which is plausible, but the only evidence offered is qualitative. No experiment separates 'better flame modeling' from 'worse background fidelity', e.g., by reporting background-masked metrics, a controlled synthetic/simulation test with known geometry, or a view-holdout study.

Only two baselines are compared, both generic dynamic-scene 4DGS methods, and both are run with author-default hyperparameters tuned for a 'flame salmon' DyNeRF scene rather than re-tuned for this data. No comparison against the fire-specific prior work the paper itself cites (Ihrke & Magnor tomographic flame reconstruction; Chu et al. physics-informed smoke), no comparison against sparse-view dynamic Gaussian methods (e.g., deformable/4D variants designed for few views), and — critically — no ablation of FreeTimeGS itself, despite the dynamic representation being the paper's main methodological choice.

The paper's own framing emphasizes that fire 'emits and refracts light' with strong view- and time-dependent effects, but the method models flames as ordinary FreeTimeGS primitives with isotropic opacity and a Gaussian temporal opacity window. No view-dependent/emissive radiance term, no absorption/transparency modeling, and no validation that the reconstruction is photometrically consistent with a volumetric medium. The physics motivation in the introduction is not matched by the model.

Evaluation metrics are poor proxies for a volumetric, high-frequency phenomenon. PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS on masked 2D regions cannot assess temporal coherence, volumetric structure, or the accuracy of the reconstructed velocity field, even though the paper claims the velocity field 'enables a variety of downstream tasks for interpreting fire (e.g., robot navigation).' No downstream task, temporal-consistency metric, or velocity-field validation is provided.

Practical methodological gaps in the dynamic stage: the flow-field initialization requires dense optical flow, which the limitations section admits is unreliable in low-texture/strongly emissive regions — precisely the fire regime — yet no sensitivity analysis to flow quality is given. The linear-velocity FreeTimeGS model is also acknowledged to be inadequate for turbulent flames, again without quantification of how much this limits fidelity.

Reproducibility is only partial: the supplement releases preprocessing/optimization code and a single example scene, with the full dataset and codebase promised for later. Given that several components rely on author-default parameters (e.g., 4DGS baselines capped at 10^6 Gaussians, 4000–5000 iterations), exact reproduction of the comparison is uncertain.

Presentation issues: inconsistent and confusing naming of the two 4DGS baselines ('4DGS (Wu et al.)' vs. '4DGS (Yang et al.)'), a typo in the metric name ('RSME_depth' in Tabs. 1–2), ambiguous captioning of Figs. 4/5 relative to the text, and a rolling-shutter delay model whose claimed sub-pixel approximation error is asserted rather than demonstrated.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely novel and underexplored problem—3D reconstruction of dynamic fire—with clear practical motivation (safety, simulation, robotics) and demonstrates that existing dynamic Gaussian Splatting methods systematically fail on this class of emissive, semi-transparent, rapidly deforming phenomena.

Provides a useful multi-component contribution beyond a single method: a real-world fire dataset (17 scenes, 400 Hz, 3 cameras), a synthetic ray-traced benchmark with ground-truth velocity fields, a novel density-weighted volumetric evaluation (DVE) metric, and a low-cost hardware synchronization setup that enables sub-frame alignment with commodity cameras.

The flow-based initialization (fusing per-view 2D optical flow into a 3D velocity field via a regularized least-squares problem, Eqs. 3-6) is a clean, principled way to initialize transient Gaussians under sparse-view underconstraint, and it is a more defensible design than relying on RoMa-style matching, which the authors empirically show fails on flames (Fig. 12).

Ablations are thorough and honest: NoSync, RandFlow, JointOpt, and NoMask isolate the individual components, and the authors transparently discuss the trade-off between visual fidelity and physical/motion accuracy (e.g., NoMask improves PSNR but degrades DVE).

Paper is clearly written, well-organized, and figures (qualitative depth and stream-plot comparisons in Figs. 5-6, 11) support the central claim that baselines produce degenerate depth and implausible motion fields, not just slightly worse appearance.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the transient Gaussian with lifetime and constant linear velocity is explicitly adopted from FreeTimeGS [89], so the core representational idea is not new. The incremental contributions (flow initialization, alpha loss, static/dynamic decomposition) are useful but modest, and the paper is essentially a well-engineered adaptation of existing 3DGS/FreeTimeGS machinery to a specific phenomenon.

The constant linear-velocity model is a strong simplification for turbulent, vortical flames, as the authors themselves acknowledge. This is not just a cosmetic limitation—it directly bounds the fidelity of the motion field, which is one of the paper's key selling points (velocity metrics, DVE), and undermines claims about 'high-frequency' dynamics.

Baseline fairness: the comparisons (4DGS, Grid4D, FreeTimeGS) are general-purpose dynamic-scene methods never designed for fire; the comparison is informative as a failure-case demonstration but cannot isolate how much of the gain comes from fire-specific design versus simply re-tuning. A stronger comparison would include at least one non-GS fire-specific method (e.g., the physics-informed NeRF [15] or tomographic approaches [36]) that the authors dismiss on computational grounds without direct evidence.

The DVE velocity metric—arguably the most novel evaluation component—is only evaluated on 3 synthetic Mantaflow scenes with no real-world ground truth, which is a thin evidence base for a metric that is central to the paper's 'physical plausibility' claim. The synthetic scenes also use simplified fire (procedural Blender/Mantaflow) whose statistics may differ substantially from real combustion.

Quantitative gains on image metrics are modest (e.g., PSNR_flame 26.93 vs. 24.48 for FreeTimeGS, ~2.5 dB; full-image PSNR 35.89 vs. 32.41), and while depth/motion gains are larger, these are measured against a monocular depth predictor rather than true 3D ground truth on real data. The overall visual improvement in Fig. 5 is visible but not dramatic.

The custom LED/ESP32 synchronization hardware, while a legitimate engineering contribution, is largely orthogonal to the core computer-vision contribution and adds a substantial systems burden that may limit reproducibility for groups without the hardware; the ablation (NoSync) shows the effect is not negligible, but the magnitude of benefit is unclear.

The reliance on dense optical flow (MEMOF) introduces the very circularity the authors criticize for flow-based evaluation—the motion prior and the motion target are derived from the same class of estimator—and the paper notes flow fails in low-texture or strongly emissive regions, propagating error into the 3D field.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely novel and difficult problem: 3D reconstruction of dynamic fire, which is uniquely challenging due to its non-rigid structure, transparency, high-frequency appearance, and rapid temporal variation. The paper convincingly demonstrates that existing dynamic Gaussian Splatting methods fail here, exposing a real gap in the literature.

Clear diagnosis of failure modes of prior work (geometric absorption, depth collapse, temporal drift) and an explicit representational shift from persistent-primitive deformation to transient volumetric carriers of emission, which is well-motivated and conceptually clean.

Well-designed methodology: separation of static background and dynamic flame, flow-based 3D initialization from fused dense optical flow, transient Gaussians with lifetime and linear velocity, and an alpha-loss to discourage dynamic Gaussians in static regions. Ablations (NoSync, RandFlow, JointOpt, NoMask) substantiate the role of each component.

Practical and creative low-cost synchronization hardware (ESP32-controlled LED strips exploiting rolling shutter) achieving ~15 microsecond precision, an important enabler for high-speed multi-view fire capture with commodity cameras.

Proposal of the density-weighted volumetric evaluation (DVE) protocol with L2 and CosSim on reconstructed velocity fields, which is a meaningful attempt to quantify motion-field plausibility where standard 2D metrics are insufficient.

Solid dataset contribution: 17 real-world fire scenes across diverse fuels (propane, wood, gasoline, cardboard, paper) at 400 Hz, plus three ray-traced Mantaflow synthetic scenes with ground-truth velocity fields, with code and data promised for release.
Quantitative results show substantial improvements over baselines in flame-masked PSNR/SSIM, depth RMSE, LPIPS, and CGVQM, and in motion metrics on synthetic scenes, supporting the central claims.

Good clarity and reproducibility: pipeline is described in detail, implementation and hardware specifics are provided in the supplement, and limitations are discussed candidly (optical-flow dependence, linear motion model, static/dynamic interaction assumption).
weaknesses: Technical novelty of individual components is moderate: the transient-Gaussian parameterization (lifetime, linear velocity, temporal opacity modifier) closely follows FreeTimeGS, and the backbone is vanilla 3DGS. The contribution is primarily the domain-specific adaptation and system integration rather than a new algorithmic primitive.

The depth evaluation uses monocular depth prediction (DepthAnythingV2) as a proxy for ground truth after linear alignment. This is unreliable for emissive/semi-transparent flames and is somewhat circular given the static reconstruction also leverages monocular depth; the reported RMSE_depth should be interpreted cautiously.

Only the three-view configuration is evaluated; scalability to more views, fully monocular settings, or scenes with weaker baselines (e.g., non-GS methods) is not explored, limiting generality of the claims.

Motion evaluation (DVE) is only possible on synthetic Mantaflow scenes; real-world motion fidelity is assessed only qualitatively. Ground-truth motion for real flames is unavailable, so the strongest motion claims rest on simulation.

The constant-velocity model cannot capture turbulent, rapidly curving flame motion; the authors acknowledge temporal blurring/oversmoothing, but this is a core representational limitation rather than a minor one.

Reliance on dense optical flow (MEMFOF) as initialization introduces a strong dependency on a component that itself degrades on textureless, transparent, and strongly emissive regions, potentially propagating errors into the 3D motion field.
The static/dynamic decoupling assumes minimal background-foreground interaction, which limits applicability to larger fires or smoke-dominated scenes where the background is occluded or altered.

Fire reconstruction, while challenging and visually compelling, is a relatively narrow application domain; the broader impact on general dynamic scene reconstruction is not fully established beyond this case.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely under-explored and difficult problem: 3D reconstruction of high-frequency, transient, emissive fire from a limited number of views. The paper motivates this well by identifying concrete failure modes (geometric absorption, depth collapse, temporal drift) of existing dynamic 3DGS methods on flames.

The transient flame Gaussian formulation (per-Gaussian lifetime plus linear velocity, initialized from a fused 3D flow field) is a sensible and appropriate adaptation for a phenomenon that violates the persistent-primitive assumption of standard 3DGS.

Practical engineering contribution: the low-cost visual synchronization scheme using an ESP32, LED strips, Gray-coded frame counters, and exploitation of rolling-shutter readout is a clever, reproducible solution for sub-frame temporal alignment with commodity cameras.

Evaluation covers a reasonably diverse set of real-world fire scenes (propane, wood, gasoline, cardboard, paper) plus simulated Mantaflow/Blender scenes, with several metrics (frame appearance, masked flame appearance, depth plausibility, video quality, and a new velocity-similarity metric).
The authors commit to releasing code and data, and the ablation study attempts to isolate the contributions of synchronization, flow initialization, joint optimization, and masking.
Qualitative results (Figs. 5, 11) suggest the method produces more coherent depth and motion than the compared baselines, which is the property the paper is primarily targeting.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The method is essentially an assembly of existing components: vanilla 3DGS for the static scene, a FreeTimeGS-style lifetime/velocity Gaussian model for the dynamic part, MEMFOF optical flow for initialization, and DepthAnythingV2/PatchMatchStereo for depth. The 'transient Gaussian' formulation is not fundamentally new, and the paper does not provide a deep theoretical or representational advance beyond applying these pieces to flames.

The central 'sparse-view' framing is overstated. The pipeline relies on dense stereo depth (PatchMatchStereo), monocular depth priors (DepthAnythingV2), COLMAP SfM, and per-view dense optical flow. This is closer to a heavily-regularized multi-view 3DGS pipeline than to genuinely under-constrained sparse-view reconstruction, so the claimed difficulty of the setting is partially circumvented by dense geometric supervision.

Evaluation methodology raises fairness and circularity concerns. The primary quantitative claims rest on self-defined metrics (PSNR/SSIM_flame with hand-designed masks, and the DVE velocity protocol), which are not validated against any external benchmark or downstream task. Baselines (4DGS, Grid4D, FreeTimeGS) are general-purpose dynamic-scene methods not designed for fire, so the comparison largely confirms what is already expected; no fire-specific methods (tomographic, physics-based, or image-based flame/smoke reconstruction) are quantitatively compared despite being cited.

The ablations (Table 1) show small and sometimes contradictory effects. NoSync actually improves PSNR/SSIM over the full method, and RandFlow/JointOpt/NoMask differences are within overlapping error bars on several metrics. This weakens the case that the individual proposed components (especially synchronization) are responsible for the reported gains.

The dynamic model is very simplified for fire. Constant linear velocity plus a single Gaussian lifetime cannot represent the turbulent, recirculating, multi-scale motion of real flames; the paper acknowledges this but does not demonstrate how much this limits fidelity in the harder scenes. The optical-flow initialization also depends on a flow estimator (MEMFOF) whose reliability on fire is questionable—the paper itself shows RoMa fails on flames, suggesting a potential circular dependency between initialization quality and the claimed reconstruction quality.

Fire removal via minimum-intensity projection assumes flames are always brighter than the background, which will fail for dim flames, dark backgrounds, or scenes with other bright elements; the robustness of the static-scene decomposition to such cases is not analyzed.

Dataset scale is modest (17 sequences, ~100 frames, 3 cameras, 15 s each), and the reported DVE metric is only computed on synthetic scenes; the correlation between DVE scores and perceptually or physically meaningful real-world reconstruction quality is not established.
